“Wake up the red in your hair”: two shampoo ad versions

What viewers noticed, in what order, and for how long, using RealEye's VAI, by gender, age and time window. 20 Nov 2026

The designs in this report

ADesign A: Profile gaze (shampoo product.png)

What it presents. A tall shampoo ad: the tagline “Wake up the red in your hair.” at the top, a red BunnyEnchantment shampoo tube (Ravishing Red) on the left, a woman with red hair who looks sideways toward the product, and the brand name banner at the bottom.

Assumed purpose. Get the claim read first, then the product, and let the model's sideways gaze lead viewers' eyes to the pack and the brand.

Open in RealEye: Heatmap ↗ · AOI report ↗ · AOI VAI report ↗

BDesign B: Direct gaze (shampoo camera.png)

What it presents. The same shampoo ad and layout, but the woman looks straight at the viewer.

Assumed purpose. Test whether eye contact makes the ad more engaging by drawing viewers to the model's face, at the risk of pulling attention away from the pack and the brand.

Open in RealEye: Heatmap ↗ · AOI report ↗ · AOI VAI report ↗

How this was measuredThis test was run on the RealEye platform with webcam eye tracking: viewers saw the images on their own devices and their gaze was recorded through their webcams.

Overall findings and conclusions

Conclusion: move the brand name into the warm zone and keep A's gaze cue, then test recall

In both designs viewers notice the tagline first, then the pack, the face, the logo and last the brand name banner, and that order does not change from the first 3 to the first 10 seconds. The brand banner is the weak spot: its VAI 14.3 in A and 8.3 in B (B is 6.0 points lower). Design A reaches the logo and banner more often; design B holds the face better. Without a recall result this is a diagnosis, not a winner.

All scores are RealEye VAI (0–100) and its three measures: Reach (how many viewers looked), Speed (how soon) and Hold (how long attention stayed).

How to read the scores. The higher the VAI score (and its Reach, Speed and Hold), the better that element is at attracting visual attention. Compare like with like, and judge each element against its role.
Viewing order, both designsTagline → Pack → Face → Logo → Bannersame in the first 3, 5 and 10 s
Brand banner VAI, first 10 sA 14.3 · B 8.3B is 6.0 points lower. VAI Reach 27.1 in A and 16.3 in B (B is 10.8 points lower)
Face VAI, first 10 sA 54.2 · B 58.4B is 4.2 points higher: direct gaze holds the face
Tagline VAI, women minus menA +7 · B +10+16 / +12 in the first 3 s

The findings at a glance

  1. strength Tagline and pack lead, in every window The tagline is noticed first and the pack second, in both designs and in the first 3, 5 and 10 seconds. This part of the layout works.
  2. risk The brand name banner is the weak spot Few viewers reach the brand name banner, late and briefly, so the brand name is mostly seen only on the pack label.
  3. risk Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand In design B the face holds attention better, while the logo and the banner score lower than in A.
  4. strength Women get to the claim first Women score higher on the tagline than men in every window and in both designs; the gap is biggest in the first 3 seconds.
  5. weak evidence Age groups other than 18–24 are small Only the 18–24 group is large enough to read; it behaves like the whole sample. Other age groups are too small to separate real differences from noise.

The findings, and the evidence behind each

Every finding states what we conclude, why, and the numbers that prove it, each linked to its table, chart or heatmap in this report and in the RealEye dashboard.

1
strengthhigh confidence

Tagline and pack lead, in every window

The tagline is noticed first and the pack second, in both designs and in the first 3, 5 and 10 seconds. This part of the layout works.

Why we conclude this

VAI Speed puts the tagline first and the pack second for all viewers in every window and in both designs (viewing order). In the first 3 s the tagline has the highest VAI of all elements (VAI 57.5 in A and 57.6 in B (B is 0.1 points higher)) with Reach near 80%, and the pack catches up by 10 s as more viewers get to it (VAI 61.2 in A and 61.8 in B (B is 0.6 points higher)). A high early VAI means many viewers look at it, soon and for a while, so the entry point is the claim and the anchor is the product.

What it means for the decision

Keep both where they are; any change to the layout should be tested against them.

Confidence: high. Both designs have more than 220 viewers and the order is identical in every window.

2
riskhigh confidence

The brand name banner is the weak spot

Few viewers reach the brand name banner, late and briefly, so the brand name is mostly seen only on the pack label.

Why we conclude this

The banner has the lowest VAI of the five elements in every window and in both designs, and all three components are low: Reach (how many looked) in the first 10 s is low: VAI Reach 27.1 in A and 16.3 in B (B is 10.8 points lower), Speed (how soon) puts it last in the viewing order, and Hold (how long) is about 1. The measured heatmaps show the bottom band cold in every audience, which agrees with the numbers.

3
riskmedium confidence

Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand

In design B the face holds attention better, while the logo and the banner score lower than in A.

Why we conclude this

Comparing B with A on the same elements and window (first 10 s): the face scores 4.2 VAI points higher in B and its Hold is 4.2 higher, so viewers stay on it longer; the logo scores 4.1 lower and the banner 6.0 lower. Attention that goes to the face is not going to the brand. The designs differ in more than the model's gaze direction, so the pose is the likely cause, not a proven one.

4
strengthmedium confidence

Women get to the claim first

Women score higher on the tagline than men in every window and in both designs; the gap is biggest in the first 3 seconds.

Why we conclude this

Women minus men on the tagline is +15.6 in A and +12.1 in B in the first 3 s, and +7.2 and +10.4 in the first 10 s, mainly through Speed: women notice the claim sooner. In A, men score higher on the face early (27.8 against 19.0 in the first 3 s), so the two groups open the image differently.

5
weak evidencehigh confidence

Age groups other than 18–24 are small

Only the 18–24 group is large enough to read; it behaves like the whole sample. Other age groups are too small to separate real differences from noise.

Why we conclude this

18–24 viewers number 82 (A) and 83 (B). The 25–34 groups have 28 and 31 viewers and the 35+ groups fewer than 15, below the 30-viewer threshold for a stable score. Differences seen in those groups are marked † in the tables and are hypotheses to test, not findings.

Evidence, with links to the data

What it means for the decision

To read age effects, recruit more viewers aged 25 and over before drawing conclusions.

Confidence: high. The limit is the sample size, not the effect.

Conclusions

Keep the tagline and the pack where they are

The tagline is the entry point and the pack the anchor; they already lead the viewing order.

Follows from: Finding 1: Tagline and pack lead, in every window ↓

Give the brand name a better place

The brand name is reliably seen only on the pack label. The bottom banner adds little: move the brand name into the tagline-to-pack column, or raise and enlarge the banner.

Follows from: Finding 2: The brand name banner is the weak spot ↓ · Finding 3: Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand ↓

Use A's profile gaze as the base, and test a brand-carrying direct gaze

A's profile gaze leaves more attention for the logo and banner; test a direct-gaze face with the brand name on the eye line.

Follows from: Finding 3: Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand ↓

Protect the claim for women

Women reach the claim sooner than men in both designs: do not move or shrink the tagline without retesting.

Follows from: Finding 4: Women get to the claim first ↓

Confirm with recall, not attention alone

VAI shows attention, not understanding: confirm the changes with an unaided brand and message recall test.

Follows from: Finding 1: Tagline and pack lead, in every window ↓ · Finding 2: The brand name banner is the weak spot ↓ · Finding 5: Age groups other than 18–24 are small ↓

What to do next

Move the brand name out of the cold bottom band

Banner: VAI 14.3 in A and 8.3 in B (B is 6.0 points lower). Place the brand name next to the tagline or on the pack at a larger size, or raise and enlarge the banner into the zone the heatmaps show is warm. Preserve: The tagline and the pack, which lead the viewing order.

Follows from: Finding 2: The brand name banner is the weak spot ↓ · Finding 3: Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand ↓

Use A's profile gaze as the base for brand visibility

In A the logo and banner score higher in every window (first 3 s: logo VAI 7.9 in A and 4.4 in B (B is 3.5 points lower); banner VAI 3.6 in A and 1.2 in B (B is 2.4 points lower)).

Follows from: Finding 3: Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand ↓

Keep the claim prominent for women

Women's tagline VAI is 7 to 16 points above men's in every window. Retest before changing the tagline's position or size. Preserve: Tagline position and size.

Follows from: Finding 1: Tagline and pack lead, in every window ↓ · Finding 4: Women get to the claim first ↓

Test B's face strength without losing the brand

B holds the face better (VAI 54.2 in A and 58.4 in B (B is 4.2 points higher)). Test a direct-gaze face with the brand name on the eye line or beside the face.

Follows from: Finding 3: Direct gaze helps the face and costs the brand ↓

Did the design do what it was meant to? Hypotheses tested

People who design an image usually build in a few assumptions about how viewers will look at it. These are the main ones, and what the measured attention says about each.

  1. supported The tagline “Wake up the red in your hair” is the first thing viewers read.
  2. not supported The model's sideways gaze in A leads viewers' eyes to the pack.
  3. not supported Viewers see the brand name “BunnyEnchantment” in the banner at the bottom.
  4. partly supported The model's face attracts attention without taking it away from the product.
  5. partly supported The ad works equally well for women and men.
  6. cannot tell Viewers will remember the brand name after seeing the ad.
H1
supportedhigh confidence

The tagline “Wake up the red in your hair” is the first thing viewers read.

Yes. In both designs the tagline is noticed before every other element, in the first 3, 5 and 10 seconds.

Why we conclude this

Viewing order by VAI Speed puts the tagline first for all viewers in every window and in both designs. In the first 3 s it also has the highest VAI of all elements (VAI 57.5 in A and 57.6 in B (B is 0.1 points higher)), with Reach already near 80%. The claim is the entry point, as designed.

What it means for the decision

H2
not supportedmedium confidence

The model's sideways gaze in A leads viewers' eyes to the pack.

No measurable effect: the pack gets the same attention in A and in B, so the sideways gaze does not add attention to it.

Why we conclude this

If the gaze cue worked, the pack would score clearly higher in A, where the model looks at it, than in B, where she looks at the viewer. In the first 10 s the pack scores VAI 61.2 in A and 61.8 in B (B is 0.6 points higher) and is noticed at the same speed (VAI Speed 73.5 in A and 74.6 in B (B is 1.1 points higher)). The pack is second in the viewing order in both designs.

H3
not supportedhigh confidence

Viewers see the brand name “BunnyEnchantment” in the banner at the bottom.

Only a minority do: the banner is the least seen element in both designs, and it is reached late and briefly.

Why we conclude this

The banner has the lowest VAI of the five elements in every window (VAI 14.3 in A and 8.3 in B (B is 6.0 points lower) in the first 10 s). Reach shows how few get there: VAI Reach 27.1 in A and 16.3 in B (B is 10.8 points lower), with a Hold of about 1.

H4
partly supportedmedium confidence

The model's face attracts attention without taking it away from the product.

The face attracts attention in both designs, and the pack does not lose attention to it. With direct gaze the face scores higher but the logo and banner score lower.

Why we conclude this

The face is reached by most viewers (VAI Reach 89.5 in A and 94.7 in B (B is 5.2 points higher)) and scores VAI 54.2 in A and 58.4 in B (B is 4.2 points higher). The pack is not affected (VAI 61.2 in A and 61.8 in B (B is 0.6 points higher)), but the logo (VAI 28.0 in A and 23.9 in B (B is 4.1 points lower)) and the banner (VAI 14.3 in A and 8.3 in B (B is 6.0 points lower)) lose attention in B.

What it means for the decision

A direct-gaze face needs the brand name close to the eyes.

H5
partly supportedmedium confidence

The ad works equally well for women and men.

Both groups see the same elements in the same order, but women reach the tagline faster, and in A men look at the face earlier.

Why we conclude this

The viewing order is the same for men and women. The speed differs: in the first 3 s women score higher on the tagline (VAI 65.4 for Women and 49.8 for Men in A (Women 15.6 points higher); VAI 64.5 for Women and 52.4 for Men in B (Women 12.1 points higher)), while men score higher on the face in A (VAI 27.8 for Men and 19.0 for Women in A (Men 8.8 points higher)).

What it means for the decision

Do not move or shrink the tagline without retesting with women.

H6
cannot telllow confidence

Viewers will remember the brand name after seeing the ad.

Attention data cannot show memory, but it points to a risk: few viewers look at the brand name.

Why we conclude this

Recall was not measured. What is measured is that the banner is reached by VAI Reach 27.1 in A and 16.3 in B (B is 10.8 points lower) and the logo on the pack by VAI Reach 52.8 in A and 45.8 in B (B is 7.0 points lower). Viewers who never look at the brand name cannot recall it from the image, but those who do may still forget it. A recall question in the study would answer this.

What it means for the decision

Add an unaided brand recall question before judging the designs on brand building.

Attention data can support or reject assumptions about where people look. It cannot show whether they understood, liked or remembered what they saw: where a hypothesis is about that, the verdict is "cannot tell".

What the scores mean (VAI)

VAI is RealEye's attention score for an element of the image (the tagline, the pack, the face, the logo). It runs from 0 to 100 and is the average of three simple measures, computed from the webcam eye tracking. Values are indices over the time window; they are not predictions and not percentages of total attention across the image.

VAI

Composite index

The average of Reach, Speed and Hold. Higher means stronger overall attention on the element.

VAI Reach

Breadth

How many viewers looked at it at all. Did people get there?

VAI Speed

Speed

How soon they noticed it. How early in the viewing order? Used here to rank the viewing order.

VAI Hold

Hold

How long attention stayed on it. Did people stay?

How to use it: compare like with like, and look at the three measures rather than just the total. VAI is for comparing elements, designs, time windows and audiences. Higher is better at attracting visual attention: a higher VAI, Reach, Speed or Hold means the element does that job better. Judge each element against its role, because a logo can do its job at a moderate score. VAI shows attention, not outcome: it does not say whether viewers understood, liked or will buy, so confirm with a recall or choice test.

Component patterns and what to do

ReachSpeedHoldReadingTypical action
HighHighHighStrong element: almost everyone reaches it, soon, and stays on it.Keep it. Protect its position and size.
HighHighLowSeen fast by most viewers but only glanced at. Normal for a logo; a problem for a claim that must be read.If it must be read, shorten it or give it more room.
HighLowanyReached eventually, but late: it competes with elements ahead of it in the viewing order.Move it earlier in the order or make it more salient.
LowLowLowBlind spot: few viewers reach it, late, and briefly.Relocate, enlarge, raise contrast, or remove clutter around it.
LowanyHighHard to find, but viewers who find it read it: a placement problem, not a content problem.Move it into the path viewers already follow.
Worked example: Brand name (banner), design A, first 10 s
Reach
27.1
Speed
14.5
Hold
1.2
VAI = average of the three
14.3

Only about 27% of viewers reached it, those who did got there late (Speed 14) and looked only briefly (Hold 1). The low VAI is the combination of all three, which is why the three measures matter as much as the total.

In both designs viewers notice the elements in this order: Tagline → Pack (product) → Face → Logo → Brand name (banner), and the order does not change between the first 3, 5 and 10 seconds.

How to test it next

Design
Randomly assign target viewers to one version each, in a realistic feed or shelf context, with at least 30 Average-or-better viewers per gender and age band.
Primary Outcome
Unaided brand recall and main-message recall in the same respondent, with accepted answers agreed beforehand.
Guardrail
Purchase intent.
Diagnostic Vai Metric
Brand name and logo VAI, Reach and Speed in the first 3 s, by gender and age.

How to improve the study

Ideas to get more, and more useful, insight from the next round of this study.

Different or more AOIs

Split the big elements into the parts that matter

Split the pack into the label, the “b” logo and the cap, and the tagline into “Wake up” and “the red in your hair”. Add AOIs for the model's eyes and hair, and one for the whole bottom band including the product shot.

Why: Large AOIs hide differences inside them (the pack reaches 92% of viewers, but we cannot tell which part they look at). Smaller AOIs show exactly which word or part carries the attention.

Add an AOI for any element you want people to act on

If the final ad has a call to action, a price, a claim or a certification, add an AOI for it so its VAI can be compared with the elements here.

Why: An element without an AOI cannot be measured.

More or different respondents

Collect more viewers in the groups that are too small to read

Aim for at least 100 viewers per design in each group you want to compare. Ages 25 and over are fewer than 50 viewers per design, and the 35+ group fewer than 15.

Why: Groups under 30 viewers are marked as indicative, so the age findings in this report are weak.

Know who is looking: ask gender and age before the test

About a third of viewers (74 in A, 70 in B) did not give a gender, and 40 to 45% gave no age. Make the questions required, or recruit through the RealEye panel with the target audience set.

Why: Every viewer without an answer drops out of the gender and age cuts.

Match the audience to the buyers

Most viewers are 18–24 and on a desktop. If the shampoo targets other ages or mobile shoppers, recruit them, and test on smartphones.

Why: Attention to an ad differs by audience and device.

Add a survey: questions worth asking

Ask a few questions right after the image

Short questions after viewing turn attention data into evidence about memory and choice. Ask them in this order, with the image no longer visible.

QuestionWhy it helpsAnswer type
Which brand was advertised? (open text)Unaided brand recall: shows whether looking at the banner or the logo turns into remembering the brand.open text
What was the main message of the ad? (open text)Message recall: shows whether the tagline that everyone reads is understood.open text
What was the first thing you noticed? (open text)Compares what viewers say with what the eye tracking measured.open text
How likely are you to buy this shampoo? (1 to 7)Purchase intent as a guardrail: checks that the design that gets attention does not lower interest.1 to 7 scale
How appealing is the ad? (1 to 7)Separates attention from liking.1 to 7 scale
Do you already know the brand? (yes, heard of it, no)Brand familiarity changes how viewers look at a brand name and must be controlled for.single choice
Which of the two shampoos would you pick from a shelf? (choice)A product choice is closer to behaviour than attention or intent.single choice

Benchmark against the best performers

Compare with the best similar designs

Run the same elements (tagline, pack, face, logo, brand name) on the best-performing ads in the category, from your own earlier campaigns and from competitors, with the same time windows and viewer filter. Compare each element's VAI, Reach, Speed and Hold with those benchmarks.

Why: A VAI of 14 for a brand name only means something against what a good brand name scores in comparable ads.

  1. Pick 3 to 5 category leaders and your own best earlier ad.
  2. Add them to the same study (or to a study run the same way) and draw the same kinds of AOIs.
  3. Compare each element's VAI against the benchmark and aim for the level of the best performers.

Screen many creatives quickly with predicted attention

To compare against many competitor creatives you cannot test with viewers, use RealEye's Attention Predictor to screen them, then confirm the shortlist with real viewers. Label predicted results as predicted.

Why: Predicted attention is fast and cheap, but it is not measured attention.

Other ideas

Test in a realistic setting

Show the image in a feed or on a shelf next to competing products, and for the time viewers really spend on it, instead of a forced 10 s view.

Why: Isolated viewing can overstate how much attention an element gets in the real world.

Technical appendix

For analysts and researchers: how the study was run, the data used, and the limits of the evidence.

About this study

Platform
RealEye platform
Eye tracking
Webcam eye tracking: participants viewed the images in their own browsers while RealEye estimated their gaze from their webcams.
Study
#demo Images and Video demo (2023-10-25), stimuli 5 (design A) and 6 (design B) of 15
Participants analysed
Design A: 229 viewers (12 of 241 removed for low data quality). Design B: 227 viewers (5 of 232 removed).
Participant quality filter
Only viewers with data quality Average or better are analysed.
Time windows
First 3 s (0.5–3 s), first 5 s (0.5–5 s) and first 10 s (0.5–10 s), cumulative.
Audiences
All viewers; men and women; ages 18–24, 25–34 and 35+; and every gender × age combination. Audiences under 30 viewers are marked †.
Task and exposure
Free viewing, up to 10 s, one image at a time (demo study).
Source
RealEye dashboard: AOI report statistics, AOI VAI report and fixation data, with the filters above.
Tracker precision
Webcam eye tracking is less precise than a lab tracker, so small elements are measured less precisely than large ones.

Viewers with other or unspecified gender, or no recorded age, are in the overall results but not in the gender and age cuts.

Technical notes on VAI

  • Compare like with like: the same element, the same time window and a similar number of viewers (N). Large elements, and elements that overlap others, naturally score higher.
  • Windows are cumulative. "First 3 s" is 0.5–3 s, "first 5 s" is 0.5–5 s and "first 10 s" is 0.5–10 s. The first 0.5 s is skipped to reduce the effect of where viewers happened to be looking when the image appeared. Reach and Speed can only rise as the window grows; Hold is relative to the window, so it can fall even when viewers keep looking.
  • Small groups are noisy. Audiences with fewer than 30 viewers are marked † and should be read as anecdotal.
  • VAI is the equal-weight mean of Reach, Speed and Hold and is not a share of the image's attention.

Evidence and limits

  • No survey or choice data were available, so nothing here shows recall, liking, preference or intent. VAI measures attention only.
  • Webcam eye tracking has less spatial precision than a lab tracker, so small AOIs are measured less precisely than large ones, and AOIs are not directly comparable by size.
  • Only viewers with data quality Average or better are analysed (A: 229 of 241, B: 227 of 232). The embedded dashboard AOI VAI report cannot be quality-filtered and covers all participants with data.
  • Both images sit in the same 15-stimulus study with different viewer counts, so groups probably overlap and order effects are possible; comparisons are indicative.
  • About a third of viewers have other or unspecified gender and about half have no recorded age; they are in the overall results but not in the audience cuts. Audiences under 30 viewers are anecdotal.
  • Heatmaps by audience are drawn from the same fixation data as the dashboard, each scaled to its own maximum; the dashboard's own heatmap is shown for all viewers.
  • Viewing order is a relative hierarchy across viewers (VAI Speed), not an individual scan path. AOI shapes were used as saved on each image and are not identical between the two images.

What would change the recommendation

  • A recall result that favours B.
  • A larger sample showing a reliable age gap.
  • A test with the brand name moved showing no gain in banner or logo VAI.

Definitions

VAI
RealEye's Visual Attention Index (0–100): the equal-weight mean of Reach, Speed and Hold. A relative score, not a share of viewers or of attention. Read more on RealEye ↗
Reach
Share of viewers who looked at the AOI at least once in the window. Read more on RealEye ↗
Speed
How soon the AOI is noticed after it becomes visible. Used to rank the viewing order. Read more on RealEye ↗
Hold
How long attention stays on the AOI relative to the window. Read more on RealEye ↗
Viewing order
AOIs ranked by VAI Speed: a relative hierarchy across viewers, not one person's scan path. Read more on RealEye ↗
AOI
Area of Interest: a saved region of the image (tagline, pack, face, logo, brand name). Read more on RealEye ↗
Windows
First 3, 5 and 10 s are cumulative and start at 0.5 s. Read more on RealEye ↗
Webcam eye tracking
Gaze estimated from participants' own webcams in the RealEye platform. It shows where attention concentrates, with less precision than lab trackers. Read more on RealEye ↗
Quality filter
Only viewers with data quality Average or better are analysed. Read more on RealEye ↗
Heatmap
A picture of where viewers looked: warm colours (yellow, orange, red) mark where attention concentrated, cool colours where it did not. Read more on RealEye ↗
Gender and age
Viewers' own answers to the gender and age questions of the study. Audience groups under 30 viewers are indicative only. Read more on RealEye ↗
RealEye
The online research platform with webcam eye tracking that ran this study and produced every number here. Read more on RealEye ↗

How the data was analysed

Metric
VAI = equal-weight mean of Reach, Speed and Hold (0–100)
Time windows
first 3 s (0.5–3 s), first 5 s (0.5–5 s) and first 10 s (0.5–10 s), cumulative
Viewer filter
Data quality Average or better (grade 3 or higher; grades: 1 Very low, 2 Low, 3 Average, 4 Good, 5 Very good, 6 Perfect)
Audiences
All, Men, Women, 18–24, 25–34, 35+, Men 18–24, Men 25–34, Men 35+, Women 18–24, Women 25–34, Women 35+
Small audiences
fewer than 30 viewers: indicative only
Element order
Tagline, Pack (product), Face, Logo, Brand name (banner)

How to run this study again

  1. Create a new study in RealEye (Images and Videos) at https://app.realeye.io.
  2. Upload the stimulus images (download them above), in this order: design A (shampoo product.png); design B (shampoo camera.png).
  3. Set each stimulus' options as listed under Study set-up (display time, how it finishes, instructions, order).
  4. Open each stimulus' AOI editor and draw the elements from the tables above, using the pixel coordinates (image size as shown). Keep the same names and, if you want the new report to look the same, the same colours.
  5. Add the participant questions (at least gender and age) so audience cuts work: gender and age.
  6. Invite participants: share the study link with your own participants or order RealEye panel participants. Plan for at least 100 viewers with Average or better data quality per design, and 30 or more in every audience you want to compare.
  7. When data has come in, give an AI agent that has the neuromarketing-image-report skill the new study and item ids together with this report's data (download below). It collects the numbers, rebuilds the report and can compare it with this one.

The same study can also simply keep running: collect more participants, then rebuild the report. The report always states the collection dates and the number of viewers analysed, so two versions can be compared fairly.

The assistant can then answer follow-up questions, run extra comparisons and suggest insights you did not think to ask for.
